title: Project Fundamentals & Value Delivery
sequence: Introduction. Read this first; every later topic assumes these terms.

header.html: Background for all three domains (no task of its own). Supports Process Task 1 (assess needs, complexity, magnitude) and Task 3 (value-based delivery), Business Environment Task 1 (governance, OPAs), Task 7 (organizational change) and Task 8 (external environment).

toc.title: Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Definitions

Term PMBOK 8 meaning
Project A temporary initiative in a unique context undertaken to create value. Temporary = a beginning and an end of the project work or a phase. The unique context can come from goals, environment, approaches, stakeholders. Can be stand-alone or part of a portfolio or program
Project management Applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities to meet or exceed the intended value. This does not endorse gold plating or scope creep; it means value-driven decisions that satisfy stakeholders' needs
Project manager The person assigned by the performing organization to lead the team responsible for achieving project objectives
Project management team Members of the project team directly involved in project management activities (can be just the PM)
Project team A set of individuals performing the work of the project to achieve its objectives
Project management office (PMO) Organizational entity (department or team) tasked with centralizing activities for managing portfolios, programs and/or projects
Portfolio Collection of programs, projects and operations managed as a group to maximize overall value delivery, achieve strategic objectives, meet mandatory obligations or generate income streams
Program Group of related projects and program activities managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually
Product An artifact that is produced and quantifiable (tangible goods or intangible digital goods and services)
Artifact A document or other item created to help manage a portfolio, program or project and inform the team, stakeholders and management
Output A product, result or service generated by a process; may feed a successor process
Outcome The end result or consequence of a process or project: the long-term effects, changes or value generated (positive or negative)
Benefit A gain or asset realized by the organization and other stakeholders as a result of outcomes delivered
Disbenefit A negative outcome: unintended adverse effects, costs or losses
Value The excess of financial and nonfinancial benefits over the investment gained from achieving the goals. Different stakeholders perceive value differently
Value delivery system A collection of strategic business activities aimed at building, sustaining and/or advancing an organization; portfolios, programs, projects, products and operations are all part of it
Project success The consensus view across intended beneficiaries, other stakeholders and participants that the project was perceived to have delivered value that was worth the effort and expense
Exam angle

the ECO itself reframes success beyond schedule, budget and scope to stakeholder value and accomplishment of desired outcomes. Expect questions where on-time, on-budget delivery is not the right answer.

2Characteristics of a Project

2.1 Temporary

Projects are temporary, but their deliverables often persist. A project usually ends when one or more of these happen:

  1. The objectives have been achieved
  2. A governing body, the sponsor or the team decides the objectives will not or cannot be met
  3. Resources (funding, human, physical) are exhausted or no longer available
  4. The need no longer exists because of changes in strategy, priorities or the external environment
  5. The project is terminated for other reasons, such as legal, regulatory or compliance issues

2.2 Unique context

Two similar projects still differ in goals, scope, duration, location, technology, quality, costs, risks, resources and stakeholders, so each needs a tailored approach (Topic 05).

2.3 Value creation through organizational change

A project moves the organization from its current state (optionally through a transition state) to a future state that delivers the value key stakeholders defined.

2.4 Why projects are initiated

Organizational leaders authorize projects to respond to: regulatory, legal or social requirements; stakeholder requests or needs; new or changed business or technology strategies; creating, improving or fixing products, processes, organizations or services. Every project should link back to strategic objectives and business value.

2.5 Projects versus operations

Projects Operations
Nature Temporary, unique context, create value through change Ongoing, efficient production of products and services
Scope The project's boundaries Ongoing operations are outside a project's scope

They intersect when developing or upgrading products, improving delivery, at the end of a product life cycle, and at each closeout phase or iteration. At those points deliverables, people and knowledge transfer between project and operations. Engage operations early in planning; it strongly affects long-term success and sustainability.

3Portfolio, Program, Project and Operations

Portfolio Program Project
Definition Programs, projects and operations managed as a group to maximize value and meet strategic objectives Related projects and program activities managed together for benefits not available individually Temporary initiative in a unique context to create value
Scope Organizational scope aligned with strategic objectives Includes and integrates the scope of component projects and sub-programs Defined objectives, progressively elaborated
Planning Strategic planning, priorities, resource allocation among programs and projects High-level; tracks interdependencies; aligned with program objectives Predictive, adaptive or hybrid as the context requires
Monitoring Strategic change and resource allocation Progress of component projects and benefits realization Outputs and value
Success measured by Strategic value delivery, change management success, alignment with vision and mission Collective delivery of benefits and strategic objectives Value that was worth the effort and expense: quality, timeliness, budget, sustainability, stakeholder satisfaction

Key points:

  • Programs drive organizational change; they are not merely large projects.
  • Portfolio management = selecting, prioritizing, managing and optimizing programs and projects in line with strategy, obligations and objectives.
  • All of them often engage the same stakeholders and compete for the same resources; their managers coordinate with operations leaders to keep resource allocation balanced.
  • Organizational and portfolio planning prioritizes work by risk, funding and other considerations.

4System for Value Delivery

  • A system for value delivery sits inside an organization's internal environment (policies, procedures, methodologies, governance), which sits inside the external environment (economy, competition, legislation).
  • It works best when information and feedback flow consistently among portfolios, programs, projects, operations and products (strategy flows down; performance information and benefits analysis flow up).
  • Business value is the net quantifiable benefit, tangible or intangible:
Tangible Intangible
Monetary assets, productivity, profitability, stockholder equity, market share, infrastructure capabilities, utility, environmental improvements Goodwill, brand recognition and trademarks, public benefit, acquired knowledge, compliance, reputation, employee well-being, environmental awareness
  • Projects are investments: expected value (financial or not) must meet or exceed the target threshold, or the investment is not justified. Value today also includes societal impact and sustainability goals.
  • Ways projects meet or exceed value thresholds: meeting customer needs with a new product, service or result; delivering within a performance baseline that represents a high-value outcome; contributing to community development, sustainability and ethical responsibility; improving efficiency or employee well-being; enabling the organization's transition to its future state; sustaining benefits from earlier work.

4.1 Assessing project success (two dimensions)

Dimension Question Measured by
Success of project outcomes Did we realize the intended value (now or later)? Strategic objectives, ROI, sales targets, new customers, being first to market, process or technology improvements, compliance, social and environmental goals
Success of project management processes Did we manage efficiently? Adherence to cost, scope, time and quality; effective use of resources; stakeholder expectations met

Both matter. Good management does not guarantee value (a well-built overpass later demolished), and weak management does not always mean failure (the Sydney Opera House cost many times its budget and took 14 years yet is a landmark).

5Project Environment: EEFs and OPAs

5.1 Enterprise environmental factors (EEFs)

Conditions not directly influenced by the project team that impact, constrain or direct the project. Inputs to most planning processes; they can enhance or constrain options and influence tailoring.

Internal to the organization External to the organization
Culture, structure, governance (vision, values, norms, leadership styles, hierarchy, ethics) Marketplace conditions (competitors, customers, market share, brand)
Geographic distribution (offices, virtual or hybrid teams) Social and cultural influences (political climate, perceptions)
Infrastructure (facilities, equipment, IT hardware and capacity) Legal restrictions (security, data protection, employment, procurement laws)
IT systems (task, cost, scheduling, configuration management tools) Academic research, benchmarking, trends
Resource availability (contracting and purchasing constraints, staffing, capacity) Government or industry standards (product, environment, safety, quality)
Employee capability (skills, competencies) Financial considerations (exchange, interest, inflation rates, tariffs, taxes)
Financial capability (funding options) Physical environment (weather, working conditions, geopolitical constraints)
Emerging technologies (AI, automation, blockchain, IoT)
Public health and safety regulations

5.2 Organizational process assets (OPAs)

Internal plans, processes, documents, templates, lessons learned and historical information (completed schedules, risk data, earned value data) from the organization, a portfolio, a program or another project. Two categories:

Category Examples Can the project update it?
Policies, processes and procedures Tailoring guidelines; life cycles and methods; templates (plans, registers, reports, risk scales and matrices, contract templates); preapproved supplier lists; change control procedures; traceability matrices; issue and defect processes; resource assignment policies; work authorization; verification and validation; SLAs; project closure guidelines No. Set by the PMO or a function outside the project; changed only through organizational policy. The team may tailor templates, life cycles and checklists for the project
Organizational knowledge repositories Configuration management repositories; financial data; historical information and lessons learned; issue and defect data; metrics data; project files from earlier projects (scope, cost, schedules, baselines, registers) Yes. Updated throughout the project with project information

6Organizational Structures

Structure Work grouped by PM authority PM role Resource availability
Organic / simple Flexible, side by side Low Part-time, may not be designated Low
Functional (centralized) Job being done Low Part-time Low
Multidivisional Product, process, portfolio, program, region or customer type Low Part-time Low
Matrix: strong Job function, PM as a function Moderate to high Full-time, designated Moderate to high
Matrix: weak Job function Low Part-time, not a designated role Low
Matrix: balanced Job function Low to moderate Part-time, embedded as a skill Low to moderate
Project-oriented (composite, hybrid) By project High to almost total Full-time, designated High to almost total
Virtual / network Network with nodes at points of contact Low to moderate Full- or part-time Low to moderate
Hybrid Mix Mixed Mixed Mixed

There is no one-size-fits-all structure; the right one depends on size, industry, geography, strategy and project complexity (resource efficiency, decision speed, communication paths, authority).

7Product Management Considerations

  • Product management integrates people, data, processes and business systems to create, develop and maintain a product or service through its life cycle: introduction, growth, maturity, decline/retirement.
  • Programs or projects can be started at any point in the life cycle to create or enhance components, functions or capabilities.
  • Four relationship patterns: program management within a product life cycle; product management within a portfolio; product management within a program or project; product management across programs and projects.
  • Supporting roles: the product owner keeps the backlog prioritized so the team builds valuable features; the business analyst gathers and documents requirements so scope and product match business needs.
  • Product management supplies vision and strategy; project management brings it to life by managing execution, dependencies and resources.

8Functions Associated With Projects

People drive delivery by performing functions; one person, a team or several roles can perform them.

Function What it does Typical roles
Provide oversight and coordination Aligns effort, removes obstacles, keeps focus; may involve business analysis, business case, tendering and benefits follow-up Project managers, scrum masters
Solicit and manage feedback Gathers perspectives, insights and expectations; greater need in adaptive and hybrid work Customers, end users, product owners
Facilitate and support Encourages participation and collective responsibility; builds consensus, resolves conflict, supports people through change PMs, scrum masters, team leads, business analysts, change specialists
Perform work Provides the skills to deliver the product; may use automation and AI Team members
Apply expertise Specialist knowledge that improves accuracy and quality; spots blind spots Internal or external experts
Provide organizational direction and insight Prioritizes by value, dependencies and risk; sets the course for the next increment Portfolio managers, sponsors, product owners
Provide resources Secures funding, people, facilities and authority; allocates the right personnel Sponsors, portfolio managers, functional and resource managers

Coordination styles: decentralized (self-organizing and self-managing, typical of agile), centralized (a designated project manager, typical of predictive) or hybrid/mixed.

9Roles and Competencies

9.1 Project roles

  • Project management team: may be one person. Ideally involved from initiation through closing and sometimes in post-project benefits analysis or pre-initiation feasibility. Role is tailored to the organization.
  • Titles vary. "Project leader", "project lead", functional managers, or in agile settings product owner, product manager, scrum master, agile coach, team lead, development team may share project management tasks. The essence of project management lies in the function, not the title.
  • Sponsor, customer, product owner: provide decision leadership outside the project management team's authority; communicate vision and expectations; secure resources; advocate; remove obstacles beyond the PM's authority; critical for sustainability and ESG goals. Their involvement raises the odds of success (details in Topic 13).
  • Project team: the individuals performing the work; coordination varies with approach and complexity.
  • End users and other key stakeholders: engaged continuously so feedback is integrated and end-user satisfaction is prioritized.
  • Leadership: many styles exist; leaders should switch between them. Situational leadership (directive at critical points, supportive when autonomy helps) is especially relevant.

9.2 Project management team competencies

Competency Focus
Social responsibilities Decisions aligned with the common good; ethical standards and respect for cultural and social norms; self-development and continuous improvement
Power skills People skills: adaptability, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, sound judgment, decision-making, team motivation, negotiation and conflict resolution
Business acumen Strategic thinking, alignment with organizational context; project selection criteria, industry knowledge, business case development and financial analysis
Ways of working Standards, methodologies and frameworks; choosing predictive, adaptive or hybrid; brainstorming; change management
Results Problem-solving (e.g., root cause analysis); acquiring power and authority within policies; dealing with enterprise politics (influence, negotiation, autonomy)
  • Competency development: mix seniority and expertise to create mentoring and coaching opportunities; extend responsibility to the team's professional growth (shared with functional managers, PMOs, line managers or individuals); build a culture of continuous improvement and shared lessons learned.
  • Technology impact: scheduling, automation, data visualization and AI/ML can improve efficiency and fact-based decisions. The team must ensure data accuracy and neutral outputs (avoid bias) and, with IT, safeguard project information against security threats.

10Project Management Offices (Appendix X2)

  • A PMO centralizes management activities for portfolios, programs and projects and often establishes the policies, processes and procedures that projects follow (OPAs).
  • Modern PMOs move from process-centric to customer-centric: they align services with strategy and tailor them to what customers (executives, clients, project managers, teams) value.
  • Value proposition: actual value (cost efficiency, risk reduction, better decisions, faster delivery) and perceived value (collaboration, transparency, stakeholder confidence), shaped by organizational maturity.
  • PMBOK 8 treats directive, supportive and agile PMO models as a palette to combine, not an either/or; no single model is proven best. Maturity models help assess and grow a PMO.
  • Beyond PMBOK 8classic exam types Supportive (low control: templates, repository, lessons learned, consulting), controlling (moderate control: compliance, guidance, training, governance conformity), directive (high control: manages projects directly and is responsible for results).

11Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Coordination Centralized under a designated PM Decentralized: self-organizing team, product owner and scrum master share PM functions Mixed; self-organized teams inside a centrally coordinated project
Project management function Usually a project manager Often product owner, scrum master, team lead Both
Stakeholder feedback At milestones and acceptance Continuous: reviews each iteration Both
Success focus Delivering to the baselined plan while preserving value Delivering working increments and early value; adapting to feedback Plan for stable parts, adapt for uncertain parts
Value check Business case revalidated at phase gates Value reprioritized every iteration Both

12Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. On time and on budget is not enough. If the business case collapsed (market gone, need no longer exists), revalidate value with the sponsor before continuing; a good schedule does not justify an unwanted project.
  2. Outputs are not outcomes or benefits. Delivering features is not the same as realizing benefits; make sure benefits are tracked after delivery.
  3. A program is not a big project, and a portfolio is about strategic fit. Know who is accountable for what at each level.
  4. Projects end for several reasons, including loss of need or funding. End them formally (approvals, lessons learned, release of resources), not by drifting.
  5. Operations are outside project scope. Engage operations early; plan the handover of deliverables, people and knowledge.
  6. Authority follows structure. In a functional or weak matrix the PM cannot overrule functional managers: negotiate and align them. In a strong matrix or project-oriented structure the PM has more authority.
  7. Update the right assets. Proven improvements and lessons learned go into the organizational knowledge repositories. Policies and templates are tailored, not changed, by the project.
  8. EEFs are not yours to change. A new regulation or market shift is something you adapt to (and assess for scope impact).
  9. Use the organization's defined routes (PMO resource pool, standard processes) rather than bypassing them.
  10. Titles do not decide who does project management. In agile settings product owner or scrum master may carry project management functions; focus on the function.
  11. "Meet or exceed value" never means gold plating. Extra, unrequested scope is not value.
  12. Power skills matter. Leadership, communication, negotiation and emotional intelligence are as important as technical skills (Topics 13, 25, 26).

13Exam Q&A

13.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A part-time project manager in a functional organization needs a database administrator for two weeks, but the administrator's own manager says operations work comes first. What should the project manager do?

  • AWait until the administrator's operations workload eases before scheduling the work
  • BInstruct the administrator to start the project tasks without further discussion
  • CHire an outside administrator and charge the cost to the sponsor's budget
  • DNegotiate a time slot with that manager, backed by the project's business priority
Show the answer

Answer: D. In a functional structure the project manager has little authority over resources, so access is negotiated with the functional manager, using the sponsor's priority and the business impact. Ordering the person, waiting passively or buying capacity unilaterally ignores that route.

S2Three related projects each have their own manager and schedule, yet their releases collide and the combined business benefit depends on all three arriving together. What would help most?

  • AHand the three projects to the portfolio manager to schedule directly
  • BMerge the three scopes into one large project that runs under a single combined baseline
  • CManage them as a program that coordinates their interdependencies and shared benefits
  • DTell each manager to protect its own baseline and report problems monthly
Show the answer

Answer: C. A program coordinates related projects to obtain benefits that managing them separately cannot, tracking interdependencies and benefits across them. Merging them into one big project, defending separate baselines or having the portfolio manager schedule them misses what a program offers.

S3Before sizing the backlog for a new release, the product team wants the actual effort of similar features delivered on earlier projects. Where should the project manager look first?

  • AThe enterprise environmental factors that describe current market conditions
  • BThe organizational knowledge repository that holds historical project information
  • CThe sponsor's own recollection of how much effort similar features took
  • DThe PMO's library of policies, procedures and approved project templates
Show the answer

Answer: B. Historical information and lessons learned from earlier projects sit in the organizational knowledge repositories, and past actuals support estimating. Policies and templates are rules, environmental factors are conditions, and recollection is not evidence.

S4While planning a product release, the project manager lists items that will shape the work. Which one is an enterprise environmental factor rather than an organizational process asset?

  • AThe lessons learned repository from earlier similar projects
  • BThe company's standard change control template for all projects
  • CA newly enacted data-protection law in the customer's country
  • DThe PMO's approved supplier list for hardware purchases
Show the answer

Answer: C. A law lies outside the team's control and constrains the project, which makes it an enterprise environmental factor. Templates, repositories and approved supplier lists belong to the organization and are process assets.

S5A hybrid project will hand its new service to an operations team that has not been involved so far. When should the project manager engage the operations team?

  • AAfter acceptance testing, once the deliverables are stable enough to hand over
  • BDuring the closing phase, when the handover is scheduled
  • CDuring planning, so that readiness and support needs shape the work
  • DOnly if the operations team raises concerns on its own
Show the answer

Answer: C. Early engagement lets operations influence design and readiness, so people, knowledge and deliverables transfer smoothly. Waiting for closing or acceptance leaves little time to fix gaps.

S6An organization has no project managers; it uses scrum masters and team leads. The sponsor asks who is responsible for project management work on a new initiative. What is the best response?

  • ANo one, because nobody in the organization holds the project manager title
  • BThe functional manager of the department that hosts the team
  • CThe sponsor, who must take over all coordination and facilitation work
  • DWhoever performs the project management functions, whatever their title
Show the answer

Answer: D. PMBOK 8 describes project management through its functions (oversight, coordination, facilitation and support), not through titles. The people who perform those functions carry the responsibility.

S7After a self-service kiosk rollout, queues and staff costs fall, but customer complaints rise and some regular customers have left. How should the team classify the complaints and lost customers?

  • AAs an assumption, because the plan expected customers to adapt quickly
  • BAs a disbenefit, a negative outcome to weigh against the benefits achieved
  • CAs an unavoidable side effect that falls outside the project's reporting
  • DAs an output, because the kiosks were delivered exactly as specified
Show the answer

Answer: B. An outcome with adverse effects, costs or losses is a disbenefit, and it is weighed against the benefits when judging value. The kiosks are the output, and treating the losses as an assumption or as outside reporting hides a result the sponsor needs to see.

S8A product team working in two-week sprints never learns how its work links to company objectives, and the portfolio board receives no performance or benefit data from the team. What should the project manager do?

  • ASet up regular two-way information and feedback flows with the portfolio and program
  • BSend the board the schedule baseline at the start and a report at closure
  • CLeave strategy communication to the sponsor and focus on the team's outputs
  • DAsk the PMO to stop all reporting requests so that the team can concentrate fully on delivery
Show the answer

Answer: A. A system for value delivery works when strategy flows down and performance and benefits information flow up, consistently among portfolios, programs and projects. One-off reports, leaving it to the sponsor or stopping reports keeps the loop broken.

S9A PMO provides templates, hosts the lessons-learned repository and consults on request, but does not enforce their use. Which classic PMO type does this describe?

  • AFunctional, because it operates inside a single department only
  • BSupportive, because it offers guidance and resources with low control
  • CDirective, because it takes control by managing the projects directly
  • DControlling, because it requires compliance with frameworks and governance
Show the answer

Answer: B. A PMO that supplies templates, a repository and consulting without requiring their use exercises low control, which is the supportive type. Controlling PMOs require compliance, and directive PMOs manage the projects and answer for results.

S10The PMO's standard risk register template does not suit a team that tracks risks as backlog items. What should the project manager do?

  • ATailor the template within the organization's guidelines and record the changes
  • BDrop the template and keep the risks in the team's private notes
  • CEdit the PMO's master template so every project adopts the new layout at once
  • DUse the PMO template unchanged so that reports stay comparable
Show the answer

Answer: A. Templates are process assets that projects may tailor within the organization's guidelines, and the master version changes only through organizational policy. Using the template unchanged, editing the master and abandoning it all bypass that route.

13.2 Recall Q&As

R1How does PMBOK 8 define a project?

Show the answer

A temporary initiative in a unique context undertaken to create value.

R2Name the conditions under which a project usually ends.

Show the answer

Objectives achieved; governing body, sponsor or team decides objectives will not or cannot be met; resources exhausted; need no longer exists due to strategy, priority or environment changes; terminated for legal, regulatory or compliance reasons.

R3Distinguish output, outcome, benefit and value.

Show the answer

Output is what a process produces; outcome is the end result or consequence; benefit is the positive gain from outcomes; value is benefits in excess of investment (financial and nonfinancial).

R4What are the two dimensions of project success?

Show the answer

Success of project outcomes (value realized) and success of project management processes (cost, scope, time, quality efficiency).

R5How is a program different from a project and a portfolio?

Show the answer

A program coordinates related projects for benefits unavailable individually and drives organizational change; a project creates value through a unique deliverable; a portfolio groups programs, projects and operations for strategic value.

R6What are EEFs, with two internal and two external examples?

Show the answer

Conditions not directly influenced by the team. Internal: culture, resource availability. External: legal restrictions, marketplace conditions.

R7What are the two OPA categories and which can the project update?

Show the answer

Policies, processes and procedures (not updated by the project; tailored only) and organizational knowledge repositories (updated throughout the project).

R8Which organizational structure gives the PM the most authority?

Show the answer

Project-oriented (composite/hybrid): high to almost total authority and resource availability; strong matrix is moderate to high.

R9Name the seven functions associated with projects.

Show the answer

Provide oversight and coordination; solicit and manage feedback; facilitate and support; perform work; apply expertise; provide organizational direction and insight; provide resources.

R10Name the five project management team competencies.

Show the answer

Social responsibilities, power skills, business acumen, ways of working, results.

R11What are the transition points between projects and operations?

Show the answer

New product or service development or upgrades; improving delivery operations; end of a product life cycle; each closeout phase or iteration.

R12What does PMBOK 8 say about PMO models?

Show the answer

Directive, supportive and agile PMO models are a palette to combine; no single model is universally best; the PMO should be customer-centric and tailored.

R13[Beyond PMBOK 8] Name the three classic PMO types by degree of control.

Show the answer

Supportive (low), controlling (moderate), directive (high).

14Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Project Temporary initiative in a unique context to create value
Project success Consensus that value was delivered and worth the effort and expense
Two success dimensions Outcomes (value) and management efficiency (cost, scope, time, quality)
Output → outcome → benefit → value Deliverable → consequence → positive gain → gain over investment (disbenefits are the negatives)
Program vs project vs portfolio Coordinated benefits / unique deliverable / strategic grouping and prioritization
Operations Ongoing and outside project scope; engage early; hand over deliverables, people, knowledge
Why projects start Regulatory/legal/social; stakeholder needs; strategy change; create/improve/fix
Project ends when Objectives met; cannot be met; resources gone; need gone; legal or compliance termination
EEFs Not controlled by the team (internal and external); adapt to them
OPAs Policies/processes/procedures (tailor, don't update) and knowledge repositories (update)
Structures Functional (low authority), weak/balanced/strong matrix, project-oriented (high authority)
7 functions Oversight/coordination, feedback, facilitate/support, perform work, expertise, direction/insight, resources
5 competencies Social responsibilities, power skills, business acumen, ways of working, results
Titles Function matters, not title; product owner or scrum master may carry PM functions
PMO Centralizes management; customer-centric; models combine; classic types supportive/controlling/directive [Beyond PMBOK 8]
First-action pattern Check the value case, use organizational routes, update the right assets, engage operations early
